blocks.title: Why RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness matters in a real product

spans.text: Problem statement:

A team is dealing with a RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks. They do not need trivia about RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness; they need a decision they can make, a concrete artifact they can inspect, and a way to know whether unsupported claim rate per answer is improving.

This lesson keeps one running case in view: faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks. Every module asks what the system sees, what it changes, what can go wrong, and how a reviewer would prove the behavior before trusting it.

Before reading on, predict: if the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence, which part of the design would you inspect first - input, mechanism, decision rule, implementation, or monitoring?
Because this is an intermediate lesson, assume the vocabulary is learnable and spend your effort on tradeoffs, integration points, and the tests that prove the design works.

items.text: Business framing: RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness matters when it changes a launch, buy/build, safety, or quality decision for the product team.
Engineering framing: RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness matters when it changes state, interfaces, tests, traces, data, model behavior, or runtime limits.
Validation framing: the lesson is not done until unsupported claim rate per answer can be measured on examples that look like the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks

spans.text: Scenario: a RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks. The team wants unsupported claim rate per answer, but it has already seen the failure mode where the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence.
Here is the worked artifact at the level you would bring to a design review.
Complete artifact

items.text: User-facing goal: deliver a reliable RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness experience for the running case, not a demo that only works on easy examples.
Inputs: one realistic user request, the available evidence or data, and any policy, schema, budget, or latency constraint that limits the answer.
Decision rule: choose the smallest design that can satisfy the goal and expose the failure signal. If the evidence is missing or risky, stop or escalate instead of guessing.
Output contract: return the answer, decision, or artifact plus the evidence used, the confidence or pass/fail status, and the next action for a reviewer.

Verification: run at least three cases - happy path, ambiguous edge case, and the known failure case: the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence. Track unsupported claim rate per answer before and after the change.

spans.text: A complete prompt/checklist you could hand to an AI assistant

Role: You are helping build or review faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks. Context: the product case is a RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks. Task: produce a one-page plan that states the input contract, processing steps, output contract, validation cases, and owner for each risk. Constraints: do not invent evidence; call out missing data; prefer the smallest testable design; include the failure case "the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence". Output schema: {goal, inputs, steps, validation_cases, risk_owner, metric}.
That is the standard to copy throughout the lesson: concrete scenario first, full artifact second, then mechanism, tradeoff, code or verification, and solo application.

blocks.title: Mechanism: the applied idea

spans.text: Mechanism is the part of RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness that explains why the running system behaves the way it does. For a RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks, do not start by naming tools. Start by tracing the path from input to decision to output.
Plain-language framing
Imagine the system as an operations checklist. A request arrives, the system gathers evidence, a rule or model transforms that evidence, and the result must be checked before anyone relies on it.
Engineering framing

Now translate the same flow into contracts: input schema, state carried between steps, external calls, model or algorithm decision, validation result, and logged evidence. The contract is what lets you debug the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence.
Recall from module 1: the running artifact is faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks. Which field in that artifact would expose unsupported claim rate per answer?

blocks.title: Case study: the first review meeting

spans.text: The team reviews faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks after a week of prototype use. One user-visible metric is improving: unsupported claim rate per answer. But a reviewer finds the known failure pattern: the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence.

The decision is not to throw away the prototype. The team keeps the working slice, then adds one missing control: better state capture, stricter retrieval, a clearer schema, a human approval step, or a monitoring alert depending on the failure.

items.text: What changed: the artifact now records the evidence it used, not just the final answer.
What stayed small: the team did not optimize the entire stack before proving the failure could be detected.
What got measured: unsupported claim rate per answer became part of the release gate, not an after-the-fact dashboard.

blocks.title: Design choices: the applied idea

spans.text: The design choice is rarely "use RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness" or "do not use it." The real choice is how much rigor to add for this user's risk, data, and operational burden.

In the running case, a thin slice is useful only if it proves the hardest assumption. Production design is justified when users depend on the behavior. Advanced optimization comes later, after traces show the bottleneck or failure pattern.

items.text: Choose the thin slice when the requirement is still uncertain and you need fast feedback.
Choose the production path when the failure would affect users, money, compliance, or trust.
Choose advanced optimization only after measured evidence shows the baseline is the limiting factor.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The happy path for RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness is not enough. In the running case, watch for failures that look successful until a user, auditor, or downstream system checks the details.

items.text: Silent success: the system returns an answer or artifact but hides that evidence was missing, stale, or incomplete.
Wrong abstraction: the team optimizes a model, framework, or metric when the real problem is data quality, policy, state, or workflow ownership.
Evaluation gap: tests cover polished examples but not the known failure case: the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence.
Operational drift: the design works once, then degrades when traffic, data, users, or dependencies change.

spans.text: Specific diagnostic: when unsupported claim rate per answer worsens, inspect the first step where evidence enters the system and the last step where the output is validated.

blocks.useWhen: Use the production path when a RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks affects real users and unsupported claim rate per answer is part of launch quality.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect the failure where the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: First make the failure visible, then make the system faster, cheaper, or more sophisticated.

blocks.title: Runnable check: rank evidence before generating an answer
blocks.code:
# RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness: tiny retrieval check for the running case.
query = "refund deadline policy"
docs = [
    {"id": "policy-refunds", "text": "Refund requests must include the invoice id and arrive within 30 days."},
    {"id": "brand-tone", "text": "Support replies should be warm, short, and direct."},
    {"id": "shipping", "text": "Shipping delays can be escalated after 7 days."},
]

def score(doc, query):
    terms = set(query.split())
    return sum(1 for term in terms if term in doc["text"].lower())

ranked = sorted(docs, key=lambda d: score(d, query), reverse=True)
print(ranked[0]["id"])
print("grounded" if score(ranked[0], query) >= 2 else "needs review")

spans.text: This is not the full production implementation of RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness. It is a runnable miniature that makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision, output, and a check tied to the running failure mode.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the two printed lines. Which document wins, and does the toy check consider it grounded?
predictThenReveal.answer:
It prints:
policy-refunds
grounded

The policy document contains the key terms "refund" and "deadline" context, so it should be selected before generation. In a real RAG system this check becomes a retrieval metric, not the whole answer-quality test.

questions.why: The lesson is valuable only if it changes an artifact, release gate, or evaluation tied to unsupported claim rate per answer.
questions.rot: Prefer the smallest design that exposes the failure case: the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence.

spans.text: From memory, reconstruct RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness as a five-part path: the concrete problem (a RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks), the mechanism, the design choice, the implementation or verification check, and the failure mode (the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence). Then name the metric that tells you whether the work improved: unsupported claim rate per answer.

capstone.prompt: Create a one-page plan for faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks. Include the problem, inputs, mechanism, design choice, runnable or reviewable check, metric (unsupported claim rate per answer), known failure (the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence), and the next rung you would study or build after this lesson.
